The three scripts, and what each one is:
Japanese is written with three scripts at once, in the same sentence, and which one a word takes is part of the word. Nothing here is optional or alternative — a sentence uses all three because each does a different job.

| Script | Characters | What it writes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hiragana | 46 basic | Grammar, and native words with no kanji |
| Katakana | 46 basic | Foreign words, names, emphasis, sound effects |
| Kanji | ~2,136 in common use | The meaningful core of most words |

Take 私は日本語を勉強します。

- 私 (I), 日本語 (Japanese language) and 勉強 (study) are **kanji** — the content.
- は and を are **hiragana** — the particles that say who is doing what.
- します is **hiragana** — the verb ending that carries the tense and politeness.

**Hiragana and katakana are the same 46 sounds.** They are two alphabets for one set of syllables: あ and ア are both *a*. So learning the second is learning new shapes, not new sounds, which is why they come one after the other rather than together.

**There are no spaces.** The change of script is what separates words — kanji block, hiragana ending, kanji block. That is one of the reasons reading in all-hiragana is harder than it looks, and why learning kanji is not optional for reading.

**Romaji — Japanese in Latin letters — is not a fourth script.** It is a crutch for foreigners and it is not used in Japan except on signs aimed at tourists. Every lesson from here on gives kana, and romaji only where the point is about pronunciation.

**Practice.** Look at any Japanese sentence and mark which script each character is in before trying to read it. Do that for five sentences; the shapes are more different than they look at first, and telling them apart is the whole skill this stage builds.
Hiragana: あ い う え お:
The five vowels, and the order everything else follows. Japanese orders its syllables a-i-u-e-o, and every row after this is a consonant run through those five in that order — so the order is worth knowing cold before the shapes are.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| あ | *a* | Three strokes. The one most people find hardest at first. |
| い | *i* | Two strokes, both top to bottom. The left is longer. |
| う | *u* | Two strokes. A short tick, then the body. |
| え | *e* | Two strokes. The tick again, then the rest in one. |
| お | *o* | Three strokes. Nearly the mirror of あ — the difference is the tick on the right. |

**The sounds are short and flat.** あ is the *a* of "father" cut short, not the *a* of "cat". う is closer to the *oo* of "book" than of "boot", and the lips are not rounded as hard as in English. え is the *e* of "bet". お is the *o* of "or", again short, with no glide into a *w* sound at the end — English "go" ends in a *w* that Japanese お never has.

**あ and お are the pair to be careful with.** They differ by the tick at the top right of お and by あ's crossing stroke. Write them next to each other a few times.

**Practice.** Write each five times, saying it aloud as you write — the sound and the hand go together and learning them apart means learning them twice. Then cover the table and write all five from the sounds alone. The cards for these are in the deck once this lesson is ticked.
Hiragana: か き く け こ:
The *k* row. From here every row is the same five vowels with a consonant in front, which is why the vowel order was worth learning first: か き く け こ is just *k* + a-i-u-e-o.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| か | *ka* | Three strokes. |
| き | *ki* | Four strokes. Printed with the bottom detached; handwritten it is often joined. |
| く | *ku* | One stroke. |
| け | *ke* | Three strokes. |
| こ | *ko* | Two strokes, both horizontal-ish. |

**The *k* is harder than English's** — closer to the *k* of "skip" than of "kip", with less breath after it. This matters less than it sounds; nobody will misunderstand you. It is mentioned because it is the first time romaji flattens a real difference.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: さ し す せ そ:
The *s* row — except that one of them is not an *s*.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| さ | *sa* | Three strokes. Like き with one fewer crossbar. |
| し | *shi* | One stroke, bottom hooking right. |
| す | *su* | Two strokes. The loop is the second. |
| せ | *se* | Three strokes. |
| そ | *so* | One stroke, zigzag. |

**し is *shi*, not *si*.** There is no *si* sound in Japanese: the *s* palatalises before *i* and comes out as English *sh*. This is the first of three places where the a-i-u-e-o pattern breaks, and all three are in this stage.

**さ and ち look alike, and face opposite ways.** ち comes in the next row. Write them together once you have it.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: た ち つ て と:
The *t* row, and two more breaks in the pattern.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| た | *ta* | Four strokes. |
| ち | *chi* | Two strokes. The mirror of さ. |
| つ | *tsu* | One stroke. |
| て | *te* | One stroke. |
| と | *to* | Two strokes. |

**ち is *chi* and つ is *tsu*.** Not *ti* and *tu*. With し from the last row, that is all three irregular syllables in hiragana — every other row runs straight through a-i-u-e-o without surprises.

**つ is also the character used small to double a consonant**, which gets a lesson of its own shortly. For now, note that a small っ and a full-size つ are different things.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: な に ぬ ね の:
The *n* row. No irregulars — it runs straight through.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| な | *na* | Four strokes. |
| に | *ni* | Three strokes. |
| ぬ | *nu* | Two strokes, ending in a loop. |
| ね | *ne* | Two strokes, ending in a loop. |
| の | *no* | One stroke. |

**ぬ, ね, わ and れ are the four that get confused.** ぬ and ね both end in a loop; わ and れ, two rows away, do not. The left-hand side differs in each. They are worth writing as a set of four once you have all of them.

**の is the single most common character in written Japanese.** It is the possessive particle — 私の本, "my book" — and you will see it in every other line of text.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: は ひ ふ へ ほ:
The *h* row, with one sound that is not quite an *f*.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| は | *ha* | Three strokes. |
| ひ | *hi* | One stroke. |
| ふ | *fu* | Four strokes. The hardest in hiragana to balance. |
| へ | *he* | One stroke. |
| ほ | *ho* | Four strokes. は with one more crossbar. |

**ふ is neither *hu* nor *fu*.** It is made with both lips, not with the teeth on the lip as English *f* is — blow gently as if cooling a spoon. It gets a lesson of its own in the sound strand.

**は and へ are read differently when they are particles.** Written は but said *wa*; written へ but said *e*. This is not a rule you apply — it is two specific words, and they are among the commonest in the language, so you will meet them constantly. It is the only place in modern Japanese where a kana is read as something else.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: ま み む め も:
The *m* row. No irregulars.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ま | *ma* | Three strokes. |
| み | *mi* | Two strokes. |
| む | *mu* | Three strokes. |
| め | *me* | Two strokes. |
| も | *mo* | Three strokes. |

**め and ぬ are a pair.** ぬ has the loop at the end; め does not. If a character looks like め but trails into a curl, it is ぬ.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: や ゆ よ:
The *y* row, and it has only three members: there is no *yi* or *ye* in modern Japanese. The row is short because those two syllables fell out of the language centuries ago.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| や | *ya* | Three strokes. |
| ゆ | *yu* | Two strokes. |
| よ | *yo* | Two strokes. |

**These three also appear small** — ゃ ゅ ょ — where they combine with the *i* column to make きゃ, しゅ, ちょ and the rest. That is the next lesson but one. A small や is a different thing from a full-size one, exactly as with っ.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: ら り る れ ろ:
The *r* row, whose consonant is the one English speakers most often get wrong — it is neither an English *r* nor an *l*. The sound gets its own lesson shortly; the shapes come first.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ら | *ra* | Two strokes. |
| り | *ri* | Two strokes. |
| る | *ru* | One stroke, ending in a loop. |
| れ | *re* | Two strokes, no loop. |
| ろ | *ro* | One stroke, no loop. |

**る and ろ differ only by the loop**, as do れ and ね. Four characters, two pairs, one feature: a loop at the end or not.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Hiragana: わ を ん:
The last three. The *w* row has lost all but one of its members, and then there is ん, which is unlike everything else in the syllabary.

| Kana | Sound | Writing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| わ | *wa* | Two strokes, no loop — compare ね. |
| を | *wo / o* | Three strokes. Said *o*; only ever used as a particle. |
| ん | *n* | One stroke. The only consonant that stands alone. |

**を is pronounced *o*** in modern Japanese, identically to お. It survives for one job only: marking the direct object of a verb. You will never see it inside a word — if you see を, it is a particle.

**ん is the only kana that is not a syllable.** Every other character is a consonant plus a vowel, or a vowel alone. ん is a single *n* sound, and it takes a full beat of its own — にほん is four beats, ni-ho-n, not three. That beat is the subject of the mora lesson later in this stage, and it is the single most common timing mistake English speakers make.

**ん can never start a word**, which is why the word game *shiritori* ends when someone says one ending in it.

**Practice.** Write each five times aloud, then cover the table and write the row from the sounds. Add the row to the previous ones and read all of them in order — the rows accumulate, and reading あ through this row in sequence is what makes the order automatic.
Dakuten and handakuten:
Two small marks turn the rows you already know into five more. Nothing new is memorised here — the shapes are the same characters with a mark added.

**Dakuten** ( ゛), two short ticks at the top right, voices the consonant:

| Plain | Voiced | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| か き く け こ | が ぎ ぐ げ ご | *ga gi gu ge go* |
| さ し す せ そ | ざ じ ず ぜ ぞ | *za ji zu ze zo* |
| た ち つ て と | だ ぢ づ で ど | *da ji zu de do* |
| は ひ ふ へ ほ | ば び ぶ べ ぼ | *ba bi bu be bo* |

**Handakuten** ( ゜), a small circle, applies only to the は row and gives *p*:

は ひ ふ へ ほ → ぱ ぴ ぷ ぺ ぽ — *pa pi pu pe po*

**Three things to notice.**

- **じ and ぢ are both *ji*; ず and づ are both *zu*.** They sound the same. じ and ず are the ordinary spellings and cover nearly every word; ぢ and づ appear only where a compound word causes it — つづく, 鼻血 (はなぢ). When you do not know which, it is じ or ず.
- **が at the start of a word is a hard *g*** as in "go". In the middle of a word many speakers soften it towards the *ng* of "singer". Both are correct and nobody will mind either.
- **The marks are part of the character**, not an accent added to it. が is its own kana for reading purposes and has its own place in a dictionary.

**Practice.** Read か が, さ ざ, た だ, は ば ぱ aloud as pairs until the voiced one comes without thinking. Then read these real words: かぎ (key), みず (water), ぶた (pig), でんぱ (radio wave).
Yōon: the small や ゆ よ:
A full-size kana followed by a **small** ゃ, ゅ or ょ is one syllable, not two. These are the *yōon*, and they are how Japanese writes consonant + *y* + vowel.

The small kana only ever follow the ***i* column** — き し ち に ひ み り and their voiced forms:

| | ゃ | ゅ | ょ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| き | きゃ *kya* | きゅ *kyu* | きょ *kyo* |
| し | しゃ *sha* | しゅ *shu* | しょ *sho* |
| ち | ちゃ *cha* | ちゅ *chu* | ちょ *cho* |
| に | にゃ *nya* | にゅ *nyu* | にょ *nyo* |
| ひ | ひゃ *hya* | ひゅ *hyu* | ひょ *hyo* |
| み | みゃ *mya* | みゅ *myu* | みょ *myo* |
| り | りゃ *rya* | りゅ *ryu* | りょ *ryo* |
| ぎ | ぎゃ | ぎゅ | ぎょ |
| じ | じゃ *ja* | じゅ *ju* | じょ *jo* |
| び | びゃ | びゅ | びょ |
| ぴ | ぴゃ | ぴゅ | ぴょ |

**The *i* disappears.** きゃ is *kya*, not *kiya*. The き contributes only its consonant.

**The size is the entire difference, and it is load-bearing.** きや is two syllables, *ki-ya*; きゃ is one, *kya*. In print the small kana sits lower and is noticeably smaller; in bad handwriting it is a real source of ambiguity, which is why writing them properly small matters.

**し, ち and じ lose their *y* in romaji.** しゃ is written *sha* rather than *sya*, ちゃ is *cha*, じゃ is *ja* — because the consonant is already palatal. The kana are perfectly regular; it is the romaji that is irregular.

**One beat or two?** A yōon is **one mora**, which matters for the timing lesson later: きょう (today) is two beats, kyo-u, not three.

**Practice.** Read: しゃしん (photograph), じゅぎょう (class), りょこう (travel), ちょっと (a little), きょう (today). Write each one, keeping the small kana genuinely small.
The small っ, and the beat it takes:
A small **っ** doubles the consonant that follows it — and, more importantly, it takes a beat of its own during which nothing is said.

きて *kite* (come) · きって *kitte* (stamp)

Both are real words and the only difference is that silent beat. Say *kit*, hold the stop for one full beat with the tongue in place, then release into *te*. English does this inside phrases — "black cat", "hot tea" — but never counts it as a beat, and that is the thing to change.

**Where it appears.** Before か さ た ぱ rows and their voiced forms. It cannot double a vowel, an *n*, or the *m*/*b* of ま and ば rows in native words.

| Word | Kana | Beats |
| --- | --- | --- |
| がっこう (school) | が っ こ う | 4 |
| ちょっと (a little) | ちょ っ と | 3 |
| いっぱい (full) | い っ ぱ い | 4 |
| ざっし (magazine) | ざ っ し | 3 |

**It is written small, like ゃゅょ.** A full-size つ is the syllable *tsu*; a small っ is this. いつか is *i-tsu-ka* (five days); いっか is *ik-ka*. Same two characters apart from the size.

**At the end of a word** it marks an abrupt cut-off — あっ! — and is common in speech and manga.

**In katakana it is ッ**, and it works identically: ベッド (bed), カップ (cup).

**Practice.** Say these pairs until the difference is deliberate rather than accidental: きて / きって · ぶか / ぶっか · さか / さっか. Then clap the beats for がっこう — four claps, with the second one silent. Clapping is not a gimmick; it is the fastest way to stop treating the pause as optional.
Long vowels in hiragana:
A long vowel is **two beats of the same vowel**, not a different vowel sound. おばさん is *aunt*; おばあさん is *grandmother*. The only difference is holding あ for one extra beat, and getting it wrong changes the word.

**How each vowel is lengthened in hiragana:**

| Vowel | Add | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| あ | あ | おかあさん (mother) |
| い | い | おにいさん (older brother) |
| う | う | すうじ (number) |
| え | **い** usually, え rarely | せんせい (teacher), おねえさん (older sister) |
| お | **う** usually, お rarely | ありがとう (thank you), とおい (far) |

**The last two are the awkward ones.** *ē* is nearly always written えい and *ō* nearly always written おう — so せんせい is said *sensē* and ありがとう is said *arigatō*, with no *i* or *u* audible at the end. The handful of words that use ええ or おお instead must be learned individually; とおい (far), おおきい (big) and とおる (to pass through) are the common ones.

**This is not an accent mark.** English speakers hear "long vowel" and lengthen the sound slightly. Japanese holds it for a **full extra beat** — the same length as any other syllable. ありがとう is five beats: a-ri-ga-to-o.

**Minimal pairs worth saying aloud:**

- おじさん (uncle) / おじいさん (grandfather)
- ゆき (snow) / ゆうき (courage)
- こうこう (high school) / ここ (here)

**Practice.** Say each pair above with a metronome or a tapping finger, one tap per beat. Then read these and count the beats before saying them: がっこう (4), せんせい (4), ありがとう (5), おおきい (4).
Katakana: ア イ ウ エ オ カ キ ク ケ コ:
Katakana writes the same 46 sounds as hiragana with different shapes. Nothing new is being learned about the language here — only a second set of symbols for sounds already known, which is why these lessons move faster than the hiragana ones.

| Katakana | Hiragana | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ア | あ | *a* |
| イ | い | *i* |
| ウ | う | *u* |
| エ | え | *e* |
| オ | お | *o* |
| カ | か | *ka* |
| キ | き | *ki* |
| ク | く | *ku* |
| ケ | け | *ke* |
| コ | こ | *ko* |

**Katakana is angular where hiragana is round.** Hiragana came from cursive whole characters; katakana came from *fragments* of characters, taken as shorthand by monks. That is why the shapes are sharp, simple and often look like a piece of something larger — カ is the left part of 加, ウ is the top of 宇.

**Some are nearly the same as their hiragana.** カ/か, キ/き, ウ/う and オ/お are recognisable from each other. Others — ア, エ — share nothing with their counterparts.

**What katakana is for:** loanwords (コーヒー, coffee), foreign names (カナダ, Canada), animal and plant names in scientific writing, onomatopoeia, and emphasis in the way italics are used in English.

**Practice.** Read: カカオ, ココア, キウイ, アイス. These are all loanwords you can already decode, which is the point — katakana pays off immediately in a way hiragana does not.
Katakana: サ シ ス セ ソ タ チ ツ テ ト:
| Katakana | Hiragana | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| サ | さ | *sa* |
| シ | し | *shi* |
| ス | す | *su* |
| セ | せ | *se* |
| ソ | そ | *so* |
| タ | た | *ta* |
| チ | ち | *chi* |
| ツ | つ | *tsu* |
| テ | て | *te* |
| ト | と | *to* |

**シ and ツ are the hardest pair in the whole syllabary**, and ソ and ン join them to make four characters that look like two short marks and a sweep.

The rule is the **direction of the strokes**:

- **シ** (*shi*) and **ン** (*n*): the short marks are roughly **horizontal**, and the long stroke sweeps **upward from the bottom left**.
- **ツ** (*tsu*) and **ソ** (*so*): the short marks are roughly **vertical**, and the long stroke sweeps **downward from the top right**.

So シ and ン are a pair, ツ and ソ are a pair, and within each pair the difference is the number of short marks — two for シ/ツ, one for ン/ソ.

Writing them with the correct stroke order is what makes this automatic, because the stroke order *is* the difference. Guessing from the printed shape alone will fail; this is the single strongest argument in the whole stage for learning to write the kana rather than only to read them.

**Practice.** Write シ ツ ソ ン ten times as a group, saying each aloud. Then read: スシ (sushi), タクシー (taxi), テスト (test), チーズ (cheese).
Katakana: ナ ニ ヌ ネ ノ ハ ヒ フ ヘ ホ:
| Katakana | Hiragana | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ナ | な | *na* |
| ニ | に | *ni* |
| ヌ | ぬ | *nu* |
| ネ | ね | *ne* |
| ノ | の | *no* |
| ハ | は | *ha* |
| ヒ | ひ | *hi* |
| フ | ふ | *fu* |
| ヘ | へ | *he* |
| ホ | ほ | *ho* |

**ヘ is identical to へ.** It is the one character that is the same in both syllabaries. Which it is depends entirely on what is around it.

**ニ is two horizontal strokes** and nothing else, which makes it easy to miss inside a word.

**ヌ and ス are a pair worth separating**: ヌ has a crossing stroke through the top, ス does not.

**フ, ワ and ク** are three characters built from the same corner shape. フ is a single bent stroke; ワ closes the top; ク adds a short stroke at the top left.

**Practice.** Read: ノート (notebook), ナイフ (knife), ヒント (hint), ホテル (hotel), ネクタイ (necktie). Then write ヌ ス and フ ワ ク as two groups.
Katakana: マ ミ ム メ モ ヤ ユ ヨ:
| Katakana | Hiragana | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| マ | ま | *ma* |
| ミ | み | *mi* |
| ム | む | *mu* |
| メ | め | *me* |
| モ | も | *mo* |
| ヤ | や | *ya* |
| ユ | ゆ | *yu* |
| ヨ | よ | *yo* |

**メ and ヌ differ by one stroke** — ヌ has the extra horizontal at the top. With ス that makes a group of three built from the same crossing shape.

**ミ is three horizontal strokes**, where ニ is two. They are not otherwise alike, but both are easy to skim past.

**ヤ ユ ヨ also appear small** — ャ ュ ョ — for the yōon, exactly as in hiragana: キャ, シュ, チョ. The small forms do the same job with the same rule.

**Practice.** Read: メモ (memo), ミルク (milk), ヤマ (mountain), ユーモア (humour), ヨーロッパ (Europe). The last one has both a long vowel bar and a small ッ, which the next lessons cover — read what you can and come back to it.
Katakana: ラ リ ル レ ロ ワ ヲ ン:
The last eight.

| Katakana | Hiragana | Sound |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ラ | ら | *ra* |
| リ | り | *ri* |
| ル | る | *ru* |
| レ | れ | *re* |
| ロ | ろ | *ro* |
| ワ | わ | *wa* |
| ヲ | を | *o* |
| ン | ん | *n* |

**ヲ is effectively never used.** The object particle is written in hiragana, を, and katakana is not used for particles. You will meet ヲ in stylised titles and old telegrams and almost nowhere else. Know it exists; do not spend time on it.

**ン completes the シ ツ ソ ン set** from two lessons ago. One short mark, sweeping up from the bottom left.

**ロ is a plain square** and is easy to confess with the kanji 口 (mouth) and the number 0. In running text the context settles it.

**That is all 46.** Both syllabaries are now complete. Everything after this is combinations of what you have, plus kanji.

**Practice.** Read: レストラン (restaurant), ラジオ (radio), ワイン (wine), ロンドン (London), ルール (rule). Then write the four-character set シ ツ ソ ン once more — it is the one that keeps slipping.
Katakana's own marks: ー, and the pairs t:
Katakana lengthens vowels differently from hiragana, and it has a small set of look-alike pairs that are worth sitting down with once.

**The long vowel bar ー.** Where hiragana writes a second vowel kana, katakana writes a single horizontal bar:

| Word | Reading | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| コーヒー | *kōhī* | Both vowels lengthened |
| ケーキ | *kēki* | cake |
| スーパー | *sūpā* | supermarket |
| ノート | *nōto* | notebook |

It is written **horizontally in horizontal text and vertically in vertical text** — it follows the line, unlike every other character. It is one beat, the same as any other.

**The small ッ works as in hiragana**: ベッド (bed), バッグ (bag), カップ (cup).

**The look-alike pairs, collected.** These are the ones that cause actual misreadings:

| | | Telling them apart |
| --- | --- | --- |
| シ / ツ | *shi* / *tsu* | Marks horizontal and sweep up, versus marks vertical and sweep down |
| ソ / ン | *so* / *n* | Same rule, one mark instead of two |
| ク / ワ / フ | *ku* / *wa* / *fu* | ク has the extra top-left stroke; ワ is closed at the top; フ is one bent stroke |
| ス / ヌ / メ | *su* / *nu* / *me* | ヌ and メ cross; ヌ has the extra horizontal |
| ニ / ミ | *ni* / *mi* | Two horizontals versus three |
| ロ / 口 | *ro* / mouth | The kanji is wider and heavier; context decides |

**Practice.** Read these aloud and count the beats: コーヒー (4), ケーキ (3), サッカー (4), コンピューター (7). Then write the シ ツ ソ ン group one more time — that one is worth over-practising, because every other character is unambiguous and these four are not.
Katakana for sounds Japanese does not ha:
Katakana has to write foreign words containing sounds Japanese never needed, and it does it by combining a kana with a **small vowel**. These combinations are not traditional syllables; they were invented for loanwords, and they are entirely regular once you see the pattern.

| Written | Sound | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ファ フィ フェ フォ | *fa fi fe fo* | ファイル (file), フォーク (fork) |
| ウィ ウェ ウォ | *wi we wo* | ウィスキー (whisky) |
| ヴ, ヴァ ヴィ ヴェ ヴォ | *v* | ヴァイオリン (violin) |
| ティ ディ | *ti di* | パーティー (party), ディスク (disc) |
| トゥ ドゥ | *tu du* | タトゥー (tattoo) |
| チェ | *che* | チェス (chess) |
| シェ ジェ | *she je* | シェフ (chef), ジェット (jet) |

**The logic is always the same**: take the kana whose consonant you want, and attach a small vowel to override the vowel it came with. フ gives *f*, so フ + small ァ is *fa*.

**ヴ is a genuine oddity** — ウ with dakuten, invented to write *v*. Many Japanese speakers read it as *b* anyway, and older spellings use バ ビ ブ ベ ボ: ヴァイオリン and バイオリン are the same instrument.

**Japanese still has no *l*.** There is no combination for it and there never will be — *l* becomes ラ行. "London" is ロンドン, "hello" is ハロー. Likewise there is no *th*: it becomes サ行 or ザ行.

**Every closed syllable gains a vowel.** Japanese syllables end in a vowel or ん, so an English consonant cluster is broken up: "strike" becomes ストライク (su-to-ra-i-ku), five beats from one syllable. This is why loanwords are often unrecognisable until you say them out loud slowly.

**Practice.** Decode these without looking anything up: テーブル, コンピューター, スマートフォン, チョコレート, サンドイッチ. Then try the harder direction — write "milk", "golf" and "christmas" in katakana, then check: ミルク, ゴルフ, クリスマス.
The five vowels, and why they never glid:
Japanese has exactly five vowel sounds. English has somewhere between eleven and twenty depending on the accent, and — more importantly — most English long vowels *move* while they are being said. Japanese vowels do not move at all.

| Kana | Roughly | The trap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| あ | *a* in "father", short | Not the *a* of "cat" |
| い | *ee* in "see", short | Fine for most English speakers |
| う | *oo* in "book" | Lips barely rounded, not pushed forward |
| え | *e* in "bet" | Not the *ay* of "say" |
| お | *o* in "or", short | Not the *oh* of "go" |

**The gliding is the problem.** Say English "go" slowly and listen to the end: it finishes on a *w*. Say "say" and it finishes on a *y*. Japanese お and え do not do this — they hold one position from start to finish and then stop. An English speaker saying おはよう with English vowels produces *ohayow*, and it is immediately recognisable as a foreign accent even when every other thing is right.

**う is not the English *oo*.** English "boot" rounds and pushes the lips forward. Japanese う is made further back with the lips almost flat — closer to the vowel in "book", and in some positions barely voiced at all.

**Every vowel is the same length.** There are no stressed and unstressed vowels as there are in English, where "banana" has three different *a* sounds. In Japanese, every mora gets the same beat. This is the subject of its own lesson and it is the single biggest structural difference between the two languages' rhythm.

**Practice.** Say これ, それ, あれ — hold each vowel steady and cut it off cleanly rather than letting it trail. Then record yourself saying おはようございます and listen for whether any vowel slides into a *w* or a *y*. Recording is worth more than any amount of reading here, because the glide is inaudible to the person producing it.
ら行: not an L and not an R:
ら り る れ ろ use a sound that exists in neither English *r* nor English *l*, and romanising it as *r* has misled generations of learners.

**What it actually is:** the tongue taps once against the ridge behind the upper teeth — the same place as English *d* or *n* — and comes straight off. It is a **single tap**, not a roll and not a held contact.

**The nearest thing in English is the middle of "butter"** as an American says it: *budder*, where the *tt* is a quick flap rather than a real *t*. Say "butter", "ladder", "water" at speed and isolate that middle consonant. That flap is very close to Japanese ら行.

**What it is not:**

- **Not English *r***, which curls the tongue back without touching anything. English *r* in らーめん produces something a Japanese listener hears as wrong but understands.
- **Not English *l***, which holds the tongue against the ridge and lets air round the sides. Holding instead of tapping is the more noticeable error.
- **Not a Spanish rolled *rr***, which taps repeatedly. One tap only.

**Japanese speakers genuinely do not distinguish *l* and *r*** — they are the same sound in their system, which is why the distinction is hard for them in English in exactly the way this tap is hard for us. Neither is a failure of effort; the categories are different.

**Practice.** Say "butter butter butter" quickly, then stop after the flap and add a vowel: *buh-ra*. That is ら. Run the row: ら り る れ ろ. Then say these words, tapping once each time: これ (this), とり (bird), りんご (apple), さくら (cherry blossom), ありがとう (thank you).

Record yourself on ありがとう and compare against a native recording — the word is common enough that you will say it thousands of times, and it is worth getting the tap right early rather than correcting it later.
ふ, つ and し — where romaji lies:
Three syllables are written in romaji with letters that describe them badly, and all three are extremely common.

**ふ is not *fu* and not *hu*.** English *f* is made with the top teeth on the lower lip. ふ is made with **both lips close together** and air passing between them — like blowing gently to cool a spoonful of soup. The teeth are not involved at all. Hearing it as somewhere between *f* and *h* is correct; that is because it is neither.

ふ appears in 富士山 (ふじさん, Mount Fuji), ふゆ (winter) and the counter ～ふん (minutes).

**つ is not *tsu* as two sounds.** It is one: the tongue goes to the *t* position and releases into an *s*, as a single unit. English has this sound but only at the ends of words — "cats", "its", "bits". Say "cats", isolate the *ts*, and put a vowel after it. That is つ. English speakers tend to split it into *tu-su* or drop it to *su*; neither is right.

つ appears in つくる (to make), いつ (when) and なつ (summer).

**し is not *si*.** It is closer to English *sh*, but softer, with the tongue flatter and further forward than in "she". The romaji *shi* is a reasonable approximation; the system romaji *si* is not, and that is why *shi* is the spelling everyone uses.

**Why this matters more than it seems.** These three are not rare corners — ふ, つ and し appear constantly. Learned wrong now, they are wrong in every word containing them for years, and pronunciation errors are far harder to correct than to learn correctly.

**Practice.** Say ふ while watching your mouth in a mirror: if your teeth touch your lip, it is wrong. Say つ by starting from "cats". Then say ふたつ (two things) — which contains both — and みっつ (three things), いつつ (five things). Record and compare.
Mora: every beat is the same length:
Japanese rhythm is not stress, it is **counting**. Every mora takes the same amount of time, and a word is a number of beats rather than a pattern of strong and weak syllables. This is the deepest rhythmic difference between Japanese and English and it is worth more attention than any individual sound.

**What counts as one mora:**

- A kana: か, す, ん
- A small-kana combination: きゃ, しゅ (**one** mora, not two)
- The small っ: **one** mora, silent
- The second half of a long vowel: the second あ in おかあさん
- ん on its own: **one** mora

**Counting real words:**

| Word | Mora | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| にほん (Japan) | に ほ ん | 3 |
| がっこう (school) | が っ こ う | 4 |
| きょう (today) | きょ う | 2 |
| とうきょう (Tokyo) | と う きょ う | 4 |
| しゅっぱつ (departure) | しゅ っ ぱ つ | 4 |

**とうきょう is four beats, not two.** English says "TOH-kyo" with two syllables and a heavy stress. Japanese says to-u-kyo-u, four even beats, no stress. Saying it the English way is the single most recognisable foreign-accent marker there is.

**There is no stress to put anywhere.** English makes one syllable of a word louder and longer. Japanese does not — it distinguishes words by *pitch*, which is the next lesson, and pitch is not loudness. Trying to put English stress on a Japanese word fights the rhythm and the pitch at once.

**Practice.** Tap a finger once per mora, evenly, while saying each of: にほん, がっこう, きょう, とうきょう, しゅっぱつ, ありがとう, おかあさん. The tapping is the lesson — it is almost impossible to say とうきょう as two beats while tapping four. Keep the taps even; the temptation is to rush the ones that feel unimportant, and in Japanese none of them are.
Devoiced vowels: です, した, ～ます:
い and う often go **silent** between two voiceless consonants, or at the end of a word after one. The mora is still there and still takes its beat — the vowel simply is not voiced.

**The commonest cases are words you will say every day:**

| Written | Said | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| です | *des* | The う is not voiced |
| ます | *mas* | Same |
| した | *shta* | The い is not voiced |
| すき | *ski* | 好き, to like |
| ください | *kudasai*, with a quiet *i* | |
| ひと | *hto* | 人, person |

**The rule.** い or う between two of か さ た は ぱ (the voiceless consonants), or at the end of a word after one, tends to devoice. "Tends" is accurate — it is a strong tendency in standard Tokyo speech rather than an absolute rule, and it is weaker in the Kansai dialect.

**The beat survives.** です is still two mora even though it sounds like one English syllable. If you drop the beat as well as the voicing, the rhythm goes wrong.

**Why it matters for listening more than speaking.** Nobody will misunderstand you if you voice every vowel — you will just sound careful and slightly formal. But if you expect to *hear* です as *de-su*, you will not catch it at speed, and it is in nearly every sentence a beginner hears. This lesson is really about the ear.

**Practice.** Listen to any beginner audio and count how many times です and ます appear; listen for the vowel that is not there. Then say: そうです, わかりました, すきです, ひとつ. Say them twice, once with every vowel voiced and once devoiced, and notice that the second sounds more natural even to your own ear.
Pitch accent: the four patterns:
Japanese distinguishes words by **pitch**, not stress. Every word carries a pitch pattern, and it is part of the word in the way spelling is part of an English word.

Tokyo Japanese has one rule: **a word may have at most one drop in pitch, and the first two mora are never the same height.** Everything else follows from where the drop falls, or whether there is one at all.

| Pattern | Shape | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 平板 *heiban* | Low, then high, no drop | 端 ha‑shi (edge) |
| 頭高 *atamadaka* | High on mora 1, drop immediately after | 箸 HA‑shi (chopsticks) |
| 中高 *nakadaka* | Rises, then drops in the middle | 心 ko‑KO‑ro (heart) |
| 尾高 *odaka* | High to the end, drops on what follows | 橋 ha‑SHI (bridge) |

はし is three of those four at once, which is why this is taught now and not later.

**Pitch is not loudness.** English marks a stressed syllable by making it louder and longer. Japanese changes the note without changing the volume or the length. Putting English stress on とうきょう breaks the rhythm as well as the pitch.

**Getting it wrong is rarely fatal and always audible.** Context usually rescues the meaning — nobody thinks you are eating with a bridge. But wrong pitch is the main thing that makes otherwise-fluent Japanese sound foreign, and it is far cheaper to learn each word with its pattern than to relearn a thousand words later.

**This is why pitch is in stage one.** Tofugu puts it with the kana; the immersion guides leave it until later. Later means unlearning.

**Practice.** Say はし three ways deliberately: HA‑shi, ha‑SHI, and flat ha‑shi. Then listen to 雨 (あめ, rain — atamadaka) and 飴 (あめ, sweet — heiban) and say both. The next lesson is about why those last two are hard to tell apart on their own.
Heiban and odaka, and why a particle is:
平板 and 尾高 sound identical in isolation. Both go low then high and stay there. The difference only appears in **what comes next**.

- 端 (edge) is **heiban**: 端が stays high on the が.
- 橋 (bridge) is **odaka**: 橋が **drops** on the が.

The drop is at the end of the word, so with nothing after the word there is nothing to drop onto, and the two patterns are indistinguishable.

**This is why a word's accent is learned with a particle attached**, not alone. Saying はし to yourself proves nothing; saying はしが proves everything. Dictionaries that give a pitch number assume you know this.

**How accent is written.** Dictionaries use a number for where the drop falls:

| Notation | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ⓪ | heiban — no drop | 端 ⓪ |
| ① | drop after mora 1 | 箸 ① |
| ② | drop after mora 2 | 心 ② (3 mora, so nakadaka) |
| ③ on a 3-mora word | drop after mora 3 — odaka | 橋 ② … see below |

The number is the mora the pitch drops **after**. A number equal to the word's length is odaka; a number smaller is nakadaka; zero is heiban.

**Compounds change the accent.** Two words joined usually take a single new pattern rather than keeping both — which is a rule for much later, but it is worth knowing now that a word's accent is not fixed forever once it goes into a compound.

**Practice.** Say these with が attached and listen for whether the particle is high or low: 端が, 橋が, 花が (flower, heiban), 鼻が (nose, heiban — the same sound, both ⓪, genuinely identical). Then go to OJAD, which the next lesson covers, and check all four.
Looking up a pitch accent in OJAD:
Learning a word's pitch is only practical if looking one up takes seconds. [OJAD](https://www.gavo.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp/ojad/eng/pages/home) — the Online Japanese Accent Dictionary, from the University of Tokyo — is free and is the tool for it.

**What is in it:** about 9,000 nouns, 3,500 words that conjugate, and roughly 42,300 conjugated forms, all with audio recorded by voice actors. Conjugated forms matter because a verb's accent moves as it conjugates, and a dictionary of plain forms would not tell you where.

**The four things it does:**

1. **Word search.** Type a word, get its pattern drawn as a line over the kana, with audio.
2. **Verb conjugation search.** Shows the accent of every form of a verb, which no paper dictionary does.
3. **Text search.** Paste a passage and get every word's accent marked.
4. **Suzuki-kun**, a prosody tutor: paste a **whole sentence** and it draws the pitch across the sentence, not just inside each word.

**Suzuki-kun is the part worth returning to.** Words do not keep their dictionary accent inside a sentence — phrases flatten and merge, and a word that drops on its own may not when it is in the middle of a phrase. Suzuki-kun shows that, which no word-level dictionary can.

**How to use it as a habit rather than a tool.** When a word goes into the flashcard deck, look it up and put the pattern in with it. The cost is seconds at the moment you first meet the word, against relearning it later — and "later" in practice means never, because a wrong pitch does not stop you being understood and so never forces a correction.

**JAccent** is a free offline app for the same job on a phone, for when OJAD is not to hand.

**Practice.** Look up and listen to: 日本, 先生, 学校, 友達, 食べる. Then put one sentence through Suzuki-kun — 今日は日本語を勉強します — and listen to how the phrases group.
Typing Japanese: installing and using an:
You type Japanese by typing romaji and letting an **IME** (input method editor) convert it. There is no Japanese keyboard layout to learn on a computer.

**Setting it up on Linux.** The usual choice is **fcitx5** with the **mozc** engine, which is the open-source version of Google's Japanese input:

```bash
# Arch and derivatives, which is what this machine runs
sudo pacman -S fcitx5 fcitx5-mozc fcitx5-gtk fcitx5-qt fcitx5-configtool
```

Then set the environment so applications know to use it:

```bash
# ~/.config/environment.d/fcitx5.conf
GTK_IM_MODULE=fcitx
QT_IM_MODULE=fcitx
XMODIFIERS=@im=fcitx
```

Log out and in. Ctrl+Space switches between English and Japanese by default.

**How typing actually works.**

1. Type romaji: `nihongo` → にほんご appears underlined.
2. Press **space** to convert to kanji: 日本語.
3. Press space again to cycle through other candidates.
4. Press **enter** to accept.

**The things worth knowing on day one:**

- **ん is typed `nn`** when it is not followed by a consonant. `hon` gives ほん, but `honn` is safer and always works.
- **Small kana** are typed with `x` or `l` in front: `xtsu` or `ltu` gives っ, `xya` gives ゃ. Mostly you will not need this — typing `kyo` gives きょ directly.
- **The long vowel bar ー** is the hyphen key while in katakana mode.
- **Katakana** is usually offered as a conversion candidate; F7 converts the current input to katakana outright.

**Why this is in stage one.** Typing is how you will look words up, use a dictionary, search, and eventually write. It is also the fastest way to check whether you have the kana right: if you type what you think a word is and the IME offers the word you meant, you were right.

**Practice.** Type and convert: 日本語, 勉強, 東京, ありがとう, コーヒー. Then type your own name in katakana.
Stroke order: the rules that apply to ev:
Stroke order is not a formality. It decides what the character looks like when written at speed, it is how handwriting recognition works, and for kanji it is how you will look up a character you cannot read.

**The rules, which cover nearly everything:**

1. **Top to bottom.** 三 is written as three horizontal strokes, top first.
2. **Left to right.** 川 is three vertical strokes, left first.
3. **Horizontal before vertical** where they cross. 十 is the horizontal, then the vertical.
4. **Outside before inside.** 国 is the box's left side and top-right together, then the inside, then the bottom of the box last.
5. **A closing stroke comes last.** The bottom of 国's box closes it, so it is the final stroke.
6. **Centre before the sides** in a symmetrical character. 小 is the middle stroke, then left, then right.
7. **A piercing vertical stroke comes last.** 中 is the box, then the vertical through it.

**The rules conflict sometimes**, and the exceptions have to be learned individually — 右 and 左 start differently despite looking symmetrical. That is why every character is worth watching once rather than deduced.

**Where to watch.** [Jisho](https://jisho.org) shows an animated stroke order for every kanji and kana. WriteJapanese covers all 2,136 jōyō the same way. Both are free.

**The loop that works:** watch the animation once, trace it on paper alongside, then write it from memory before checking. Watching without writing does nothing — the knowledge is in the hand, not the eye.

**Practice.** Write 一 二 三 十 口 日 中 国 following the rules, saying which rule applies as you go. Then check each against Jisho's animation. These eight are the first kanji set in the deck anyway, so the practice is not thrown away.
Writing kana by hand:
Both syllabaries, written from memory, with correct stroke order. This is the point at which reading knowledge becomes writing knowledge, and they are not the same thing — recognising し is easy, producing it on a blank page is a different skill.

**Why bother, when everything is typed.** Three reasons that survive scrutiny:

- **It fixes the look-alikes.** シ ツ ソ ン are distinguished by stroke direction, so writing them is what makes the distinction stick. Readers who never write them keep confusing them for years.
- **It is how you will learn kanji.** The kanji track ahead writes every character, and the hand needs to already know how a stroke is made before the characters get complicated.
- **The recall is stronger.** Producing from memory is a harder retrieval than recognising, and harder retrieval is better remembered.

**How to practise so it is not busywork.** Not rows of the same character — that is copying, and after the third one the hand is tracing rather than recalling. Instead:

1. Say a sound aloud.
2. Write the kana from memory.
3. Check.

Five characters at a time, mixed, in random order. Being unable to produce one is the useful information; writing it twenty times in a row hides it.

**The note panel on a card is for exactly this.** A kanji card says "read it, then write it from memory", and the panel beside it keeps what you wrote — so next time the card comes round, the previous attempt is there to compare against. That comparison is most of the value of writing by hand at all.

**Practice.** Work through all 46 hiragana from the sounds alone, in random order, then all 46 katakana. Mark the ones that did not come. Those — not the whole set — are what to do again tomorrow.
First listening: comprehensible input fr:
Immersion starts now rather than after some gate, but it starts with material made to be understood at this level. The point is not to be surrounded by Japanese — it is to understand things in Japanese, which is a different activity.

**What makes it comprehensible.** Material where you follow most of it from context, gesture and picture even without the vocabulary. An hour of a drama you cannot follow teaches nothing; ten minutes you mostly understand teaches a lot. The difference is not effort, it is whether the input is at a level your brain can map onto meaning.

**Two free sources, both from absolute beginner:**

- **Comprehensible Japanese** (Yuki) on YouTube. Video, heavily supported by drawings and gesture, graded from Complete Beginner upward. The visual support is what makes the first videos followable with no vocabulary at all.
- **Nihongo con Teppei for Beginners.** A podcast, 1,400-plus free episodes, three to five minutes each, spoken slowly with heavy repetition. Audio only, so it is harder than Yuki's videos at the start and better once a little vocabulary is in.

**How to use it at this stage.** Ten to fifteen minutes a day, watching for meaning rather than for words. Do not look things up mid-video; do not transcribe. Let it wash and pick up what you pick up. The gain at this point is in the ear — rhythm, where words end, what the sounds actually are — which is exactly what stage one has been teaching from the other direction.

**What not to do yet.** Anime with no support, films, podcasts for natives, music. All of it is Japanese and almost none of it is comprehensible yet. It will be; it is not now, and hours spent on it now are hours not spent on something that works.

**Practice.** Watch one Complete Beginner video from Comprehensible Japanese today and one every day this week. Afterwards, write down in English what the video was about — that is the measure of whether it was comprehensible, not how many words you caught.
First reading: Tadoku level 0:
Reading starts the moment kana does, with graded readers written to be read without a dictionary.

**Tadoku** (多読, "reading a lot") is a free library of graded readers from the NPO Tadoku Supporters, released under a Creative Commons licence. Level 0 is 71 booklets of very simple sentences with pictures; the levels run to 5, which is a Sherlock Holmes story. Some have audio.

**The method is in the name, and it has rules:**

1. **Start from level 0**, well below what you think you can manage.
2. **Do not look words up.** If a page needs a dictionary, it is too hard — go down a level.
3. **Skip what you do not understand.** The picture carries more than you think.
4. **Put a book down** if it is not working. There are 71 at level 0.

**Why no dictionary.** The point of extensive reading is volume and speed, building the reflex of taking meaning straight off the page rather than decoding. Stopping every line to look something up turns reading into translation, which is a different skill and trains the wrong one. Intensive reading with a dictionary comes later and has its own place.

**At this exact point** — kana known, no grammar, almost no vocabulary — level 0 is still partly decoding practice, and that is fine. Reading these is how kana recognition becomes fast instead of effortful, and fast kana is the prerequisite for everything in stage 2.

**Where to get them.** The collection is on the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/japanese-graded-readers-level-0-5-tadoku-ask), and tadoku.org has more with audio.

**Practice.** Read three level 0 booklets today without looking anything up. Note how long a page takes; in a week it should take noticeably less. That speed, not comprehension, is what to watch at this level.
The shape of a sentence: what comes last:
Japanese sentences are built on two ideas that English does not have, and almost every later lesson depends on both.

**The verb comes last.** Always, in every sentence that has one.

- 私は寿司を食べます。 — I sushi eat.
- 田中さんは東京に行きました。 — Tanaka Tokyo-to went.

Everything before the verb can be rearranged with no change of meaning, because word order is not what marks who does what. That is the second idea.

**Particles mark the role of each word.** A small kana after a word says what that word is doing in the sentence:

| Particle | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| は | the topic — what this sentence is about |
| が | the subject |
| を | the direct object |
| に | destination, time, existence |
| で | where an action happens |
| の | links two nouns |

So 寿司を食べます is "eat sushi" and 寿司が食べます would be "the sushi eats" — the を is the only thing saying which is which. Move the words around and the particles keep the meaning:

- 私は寿司を食べます。
- 寿司を私は食べます。

Both are "I eat sushi". The second is unusual emphasis, not a different meaning.

**Anything obvious is left out.** Japanese drops whatever the listener already knows, and the subject is usually obvious. 食べます on its own is a complete sentence — "I'll eat", "he eats", whatever the conversation is about. English cannot do this and so beginners over-supply 私は, which sounds strange rather than wrong.

**Practice.** For each sentence below, say what each particle is doing: 私は学生です。 · 田中さんは本を読みます。 · 猫が います。 Then rearrange the second one and check that it still means the same thing.
XはYです:
The first sentence pattern, and the one everything else grows out of.

**AはBです** — "A is B", where A is the topic and B is what is said about it.

- 私は学生です。 — I am a student.
- これは本です。 — This is a book.
- 田中さんは先生です。 — Tanaka is a teacher.

**です is not quite a verb.** It is the *copula* — the thing that links a topic to a description. It carries politeness and tense but not meaning, and it goes at the end like a verb does.

**There is no "a" or "the", and no plural.** 本です is "it is a book", "it is the book" or "they are books", decided by context alone. Beginners look for the missing article; there is nothing missing.

**です is said *des*.** The う is devoiced — the lesson on devoicing in stage one covers why. It is still two mora.

**だ is the plain form of です**, used with friends and in writing that is not addressed to anyone: 学生だ. For now everything is in です, because it is the register you will be spoken to in and the one that is never wrong.

**さん is not optional, and never used about yourself.** 田中さん when talking about or to Tanaka; just 田中 would be rude, and 私はさん is nonsense.

**Practice.** Say these aloud, then write them: I am [your name]. · This is a pen (ペン). · Tanaka is a student. Answers: 私は[name]です。 · これはペンです。 · 田中さんは学生です。
The topic particle は, and what topic mea:
は is written *ha* and said ***wa*** when it is a particle. It is the first of the two irregular readings in the language and it is in nearly every sentence, so it stops feeling odd quickly.

**What a topic is.** は does not mark the subject. It marks **what the sentence is about** — the thing already on the table, which the rest of the sentence then says something about. A literal rendering is "as for X":

- 私は学生です。 — As for me, student.
- 今日は暑いです。 — As for today, hot.

That second one has no subject at all in the English sense. The sentence is simply *about* today.

**The topic is usually dropped once it is established.** In a conversation about Tanaka, you say 田中さんは学生です once and then just 日本人です — "is Japanese" — because the topic has not changed. English repeats "he"; Japanese does not repeat anything.

**は carries a quiet contrast.** Marking something as the topic implies the others might be different. 私はコーヒーです at a café means "I'll have coffee" with a hint of "whatever the rest of you are having". That contrast is why は and が are not interchangeable, which gets a lesson of its own later in this stage.

**Where は goes.** Immediately after the word it marks, and it **replaces** が or を rather than joining them. Never 私はが.

**Practice.** Translate and check: As for tomorrow (明日), it is a holiday (休み). · As for this, it is my book. · As for Tanaka, he is a teacher. Answers: 明日は休みです。 · これは私の本です。 · 田中さんは先生です。
Questions with か:
Any statement becomes a question by putting か at the end. Nothing else changes — no word order, no auxiliary verb, no rising intonation required.

- 田中さんは学生です。 — Tanaka is a student.
- 田中さんは学生です**か**。 — Is Tanaka a student?

**There is no inversion.** English swaps "you are" to "are you"; Japanese does not move anything. This is one of the genuinely easy things about the language.

**The question mark is optional.** Japanese writing ends the sentence with 。 and か does the work. A question mark appears in casual writing and manga; it is not needed.

**Answering.** はい (yes) and いいえ (no), then the sentence:

- はい、学生です。
- いいえ、学生じゃないです。

**そうです** — "that's right" — is the common short answer to a yes/no question about a noun: はい、そうです。 It does not work for questions about verbs, where you repeat the verb instead.

**Question words go where the answer would go.** This is the other easy thing:

- これは**何**ですか。 — What is this? (何 sits where 本 would)
- 田中さんは**どこ**ですか。 — Where is Tanaka?

No moving the word to the front, as English does with "what" and "where".

**か also makes a question softer** when it tails a statement in conversation, and that is why です alone can sound blunt.

**Practice.** Turn these into questions and answer each one twice, yes and no: これは本です。 · 田中さんは先生です。 · 日本語は難しい(むずかしい)です。
じゃないです — saying it is not:
The negative of です. There are four ways to say it and they differ only in how formal they are.

| Form | Register |
| --- | --- |
| じゃないです | Normal polite. Use this one. |
| じゃありません | Slightly more formal |
| ではないです | Formal, written |
| ではありません | Most formal, written or careful speech |

- 私は学生です。 → 私は学生**じゃないです**。 — I am not a student.
- これは本じゃないです。 — This is not a book.

**じゃ is a contraction of では.** The written form is では and the spoken one is じゃ, in exactly the way "is not" becomes "isn't". Both are correct; じゃ is what people say.

**The は in では is the topic particle**, said *wa*, which is why ではないです is *de wa nai desu*. The construction is literally "as for being that, it is not".

**Answering a question in the negative:**

- 田中さんは先生ですか。 — Is Tanaka a teacher?
- いいえ、先生じゃないです。学生です。 — No, he's not a teacher. He's a student.

Notice that the topic is dropped in the answer. Repeating 田中さんは would sound laboured.

**Practice.** Negate each: これはペンです。 · 私は日本人です。 · 今日は休みです。 Then answer "いいえ" to the question 日本人ですか and say what you are instead.
でした and じゃなかった — the past:
です in the past, and its negative. Four forms, and they are the ones you already know with the endings changed.

| | Present | Past |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | です | **でした** |
| Negative | じゃないです | **じゃなかったです** |

- 田中さんは先生でした。 — Tanaka was a teacher.
- 昨日(きのう)は休みじゃなかったです。 — Yesterday was not a holiday.

**じゃありませんでした** is the more formal negative past, built the other way — from じゃありません plus でした. Both are correct; じゃなかったです is what is said.

**Tense sits at the end of the sentence and nowhere else.** English marks the past on the verb and then sometimes again elsewhere; Japanese marks it once, on the last word, and everything before it is unchanged.

**です has no future form.** 明日は休みです is "tomorrow is a holiday" — the time word does the work. There are only two tenses in Japanese, past and non-past, and the non-past covers both present and future. This is worth absorbing now because it applies to every verb in the language.

**Practice.** Put these into the past, then into the past negative: これは私の本です。 · 田中さんは学生です。 · 今日は暑いです。 Careful with the last one — it is an adjective, not a noun, and adjectives conjugate differently. It gets its own lesson shortly; for now, notice that 暑いでした is wrong and see whether you can guess why.
これ それ あれ, and この その あの:
Japanese has a four-way system for pointing at things, built on three distances plus a question word. It is completely regular, which makes it one of the best-value things to learn early.

| | Near me | Near you | Away from both | Which? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Thing | **これ** | **それ** | **あれ** | **どれ** |
| + noun | **この**本 | **その**本 | **あの**本 | **どの**本 |
| Place | **ここ** | **そこ** | **あそこ** | **どこ** |
| Direction | **こちら** | **そちら** | **あちら** | **どちら** |

The pattern is the first letter: こ near me, そ near you, あ away from both, ど the question. This is called the ko-so-a-do system and it recurs throughout the language.

**これ and この are not interchangeable.** これ is a pronoun and stands alone; この must be followed by a noun.

- これは本です。 — This is a book. ✓
- この本は面白い(おもしろい)です。 — This book is interesting. ✓
- これ本は… ✗

**それ is near the listener, not merely "that".** English "that" covers both それ and あれ. If the thing is in the other person's hands, it is それ; if it is across the room from both of you, it is あれ.

**こちら and そちら are also the polite words for people and directions** — こちらは田中さんです is how you introduce someone, and it is more polite than この人.

**どちら is also the polite "which of two"**, and in shops it means "which way".

**Practice.** Hold a pen and say これはペンです。 Point at something across the room: あれは…。 Ask someone holding something: それは何ですか。 Then do the この/その/あの versions with a noun attached.
だれ なに どこ どれ いつ — the question words:
The question words, which all slot into the position the answer would occupy.

| Word | Means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **何** (なに / なん) | what | これは何ですか。 |
| **誰** (だれ) | who | あの人は誰ですか。 |
| **どこ** | where | トイレはどこですか。 |
| **いつ** | when | 試験(しけん)はいつですか。 |
| **どれ** | which one | あなたの本はどれですか。 |
| **どうして / なぜ** | why | どうしてですか。 |
| **どう** | how | 日本はどうですか。 |
| **いくら** | how much | これはいくらですか。 |
| **いくつ** | how many | いくつですか。 |

**何 is read なん before です and before counters**, and なに elsewhere. 何ですか is *nan desu ka*; 何を (what, as an object) is *nani o*. There is no rule to derive it from — it follows the sound that comes next, and it is learned by hearing it.

**どなた is the polite 誰.** Use it when asking about someone you should be respectful about.

**Question words never take は.** They take が when they are the subject, because は marks what is already known and a question word is by definition unknown: 誰**が**来ますか, not 誰は. This is the first genuinely useful rule about は versus が, and it is absolute.

**Practice.** Ask: What is this? · Who is that person over there? · Where is the station (駅, えき)? · When is the test? · How much is this? Answers: これは何ですか。 · あの人は誰ですか。 · 駅はどこですか。 · 試験はいつですか。 · これはいくらですか。
の, and how it links two nouns:
の joins two nouns, with the first one describing the second. It is the single most common character in written Japanese and it does far more than possession.

**AのB — B belonging to, or characterised by, A.**

| Japanese | English | What の is doing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 私の本 | my book | possession |
| 日本の車 | a Japanese car | origin |
| 日本語の先生 | a Japanese teacher | subject taught |
| 大学の学生 | a university student | belonging |
| 木の机(つくえ) | a wooden desk | material |

**The order is the opposite of English's "of".** 日本の車 is "car of Japan" — the modifier comes first, the thing comes last. Every の chain reads right-to-left into English: 私の日本語の先生 is "my Japanese teacher", literally "me-の-Japanese-の-teacher".

**Chains are normal.** 東京の大学の学生 — a student at a university in Tokyo. Three nouns, two の.

**の can stand in for a noun already mentioned.** Asked whose book this is: 私のです — "it's mine". The 本 is dropped and の carries it.

**Do not use の between an adjective and a noun.** 高いの本 is wrong; it is 高い本. の joins nouns, and an adjective attaches directly. This is one of the commonest beginner errors and it comes from thinking of の as "of".

**Practice.** Build: my teacher · a Japanese book · my university's library (図書館, としょかん) · Tanaka's car. Answers: 私の先生 · 日本の本 · 私の大学の図書館 · 田中さんの車。
も — too, also:
も means "too", "also" or "either", and it **replaces** は, が or を rather than joining them.

- 私は学生です。 — I am a student.
- 田中さん**も**学生です。 — Tanaka is a student too.

**It replaces the particle, and that is the thing to get right.** Not 田中さんはも and not 田中さんもは. The same applies to を:

- 本を読みます。 → 新聞(しんぶん)**も**読みます。 — I read newspapers too.

**With に and で it attaches instead of replacing**: 東京に**も**行きました — "I went to Tokyo as well". The rule is that も replaces は, が and を, and follows the others.

**In a negative sentence it means "either".**

- 私も学生じゃないです。 — I'm not a student either.

**も…も… means "both … and", or in the negative "neither … nor".**

- 田中さんも山田さんも学生です。 — Both Tanaka and Yamada are students.
- 肉(にく)も魚(さかな)も食べません。 — I eat neither meat nor fish.

**Practice.** Say: I am Japanese too. · This is also my book. · I don't drink coffee either (コーヒーを飲みません). Answers: 私も日本人です。 · これも私の本です。 · コーヒーも飲みません。
ね and よ — what the end of a sentence doe:
Two small particles at the end of a sentence, which carry most of the social work in spoken Japanese. Leaving them out is not wrong, but it makes speech sound flat and oddly official.

**ね seeks agreement.** It is close to English "isn't it?" or "right?" — it assumes the listener already shares the view.

- 暑いですね。 — Hot, isn't it.
- 日本語は難しいですね。 — Japanese is hard, isn't it.

**よ supplies information** the listener does not have. It can be insistent, so it is used carefully.

- その店(みせ)は休みですよ。 — That shop's closed, you know.
- 違いますよ。 — That's not right. (firm)

**The difference matters.** 田中さんは先生ですね expects you to know that already; 田中さんは先生ですよ is telling you. Using よ for something the listener obviously knows sounds patronising; using ね for something they cannot know sounds odd.

**よね combines both** — "it's X, right?" — stating something while checking: 明日ですよね。

**ね is also a conversational filler** at the start or middle of a sentence, roughly "you know". You will hear it constantly.

**This is register, not grammar**, and it is the first thing in this stage that is about sounding natural rather than being correct. Both are worth having; only one of them shows up in a textbook exercise.

**Practice.** Listen to any Comprehensible Japanese video and count the ね and よ in two minutes. Then say: It's cold, isn't it (寒いです). · This is my book, you know. Answers: 寒いですね。 · これは私の本ですよ。
Numbers 1 to 10:
Japanese has **two** sets of numbers for one to ten, and which you use depends on what you are counting. Both are needed and both are worth learning now.

| | Sino-Japanese | Native Japanese |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | いち | ひとつ |
| 2 | に | ふたつ |
| 3 | さん | みっつ |
| 4 | **し / よん** | よっつ |
| 5 | ご | いつつ |
| 6 | ろく | むっつ |
| 7 | **しち / なな** | ななつ |
| 8 | はち | やっつ |
| 9 | **く / きゅう** | ここのつ |
| 10 | じゅう | とお |

**The Sino-Japanese set** (left) came from Chinese and is used with counters, for arithmetic, phone numbers, and prices.

**The native set** (right) is the general counter — the one for things with no specific counter of their own. りんごを三つください — three apples, please. It only goes to ten; past that, everyone uses the Sino-Japanese numbers.

**Four, seven and nine have two readings each**, and choosing wrongly is the main difficulty here:

- **4** is よん far more often than し, because し is also the reading of 死 (death).
- **7** is なな more often than しち, partly because しち and いち sound alike over a phone.
- **9** is きゅう more often than く.

The older readings survive in fixed phrases and in times: 四時 is **よ**じ (four o'clock), 七時 is **しち**じ, 九時 is **く**じ. Those have to be learned as words rather than derived.

**Practice.** Count aloud one to ten in both sets. Then say your phone number, which uses the Sino-Japanese set digit by digit. Then ask for three of something: 三つください。
Numbers past ten, and the readings that:
Past ten the system is completely regular, and then a handful of sound changes break it in places you will meet daily.

**The regular part.** Build any number by saying its parts:

- 11 = 十一 じゅういち (ten-one)
- 25 = 二十五 にじゅうご (two-ten-five)
- 100 = 百 ひゃく
- 365 = 三百六十五 さんびゃくろくじゅうご

**The big units:**

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 百 | ひゃく | 100 |
| 千 | せん | 1,000 |
| 万 | まん | 10,000 |
| 億 | おく | 100,000,000 |

**万 is the one that trips English speakers.** Japanese groups by **four** digits, not three. 10,000 is 一万 — one *man* — and 100,000 is 十万, ten *man*. A million is 百万, a hundred *man*. Converting requires rethinking the grouping, not just the words, and it stays awkward for a long time.

**The sound changes.** These are not optional and they are in common numbers:

| Number | Expected | Actual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 300 | さんひゃく | **さんびゃく** |
| 600 | ろくひゃく | **ろっぴゃく** |
| 800 | はちひゃく | **はっぴゃく** |
| 3,000 | さんせん | **さんぜん** |
| 8,000 | はちせん | **はっせん** |
| 1,000 | いちせん | **せん** (no いち) |

**百 and 千 take no 一** on their own — 百 is a hundred, not 一百. But 万 does: 10,000 is 一万, never just 万.

**Practice.** Say: 15, 48, 230, 600, 1,000, 3,000, 10,000, 25,000. Then say this year as a number. Then practise the one that stays hard: what is 百万 in English, and what is "fifty thousand" in Japanese? (A million; 五万.)
Counters, and why Japanese has them:
Japanese cannot count a bare noun. You do not say "three book" — you say "book, three *volumes*", with a word that classifies what is being counted. English does this only for uncountable things: three *sheets* of paper, two *loaves* of bread. Japanese does it for everything.

**The shape is normally: noun + を + number + counter.**

- 本を三冊(さんさつ)買いました。 — I bought three books.
- りんごを二つください。 — Two apples, please.

**Why they exist.** A counter says what *kind* of thing is being counted, and the choice carries meaning — the same object can take different counters depending on how it is being thought of. A rabbit is counted with 羽, the counter for birds, for historical reasons nobody is fully agreed on. This is one of the places where the language is simply learned rather than derived.

**There are hundreds and you need about ten.** The common ones get their own lesson next. The escape hatch is the native number set — ひとつ ふたつ みっつ — which counts almost anything concrete when you do not know the right counter, up to ten. Using it is slightly less precise and completely acceptable.

**Counters attach to the Sino-Japanese numbers** and often cause sound changes at the join, which is the real difficulty — 一本 is いっぽん, not いちほん. Those changes are regular enough to learn as patterns and are covered with each counter.

**Where the counter goes.** After the particle, not attached to the noun:

- 本を三冊読みました。 ✓
- 三冊の本を読みました。 ✓ (also fine, slightly more formal)
- 三冊本を… ✗

**Practice.** For now, use ひとつ to ここのつ for anything you cannot count properly: りんごを三つ、ペンを二つ。 Then look at the next lesson and notice how much of the difficulty is sound changes rather than vocabulary.
つ and 個 — the general counters:
The two counters that get you through almost anything.

**～つ, the native set**, counts concrete objects of no particular shape, up to ten:

| | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ひとつ | ふたつ | みっつ | よっつ | いつつ |
| むっつ | ななつ | やっつ | ここのつ | **とお** |

Note that ten is とお and has no つ. Past ten, switch to Sino-Japanese numbers with 個 or whatever the right counter is.

**～個(こ)** counts small, roughly round things — fruit, eggs, stones — and is the general fallback past ten:

一個、二個、三個… 十個(じゅっこ)、十一個

**The sound changes for 個:** 一個 いっこ, 六個 ろっこ, 八個 はっこ, 十個 じゅっこ. The pattern — 1, 6, 8, 10 doubling the consonant — recurs with almost every counter beginning with か, さ, た or は sounds, so it is worth noticing as a pattern now rather than as four exceptions each time.

**How many?** いくつ for the ～つ counter, 何個 for 個.

- りんごはいくつありますか。 — How many apples are there?

**つ is the safe default.** If you do not know the counter for something, ～つ is understood and natural. Nobody thinks less of a learner for it, and it is better than guessing wrongly at 本 or 枚.

**Practice.** Count from one to ten in the native set until it is automatic — it is irregular enough that it needs saying aloud rather than reading. Then order three of something in a shop: すみません、[thing]を三つください。
人, 本, 枚, 匹 — the common specific ones:
Four counters that cover most of what you will need, and the sound changes that come with them.

**～人(にん) — people**

一人 **ひとり** · 二人 **ふたり** · 三人 さんにん · 四人 **よにん** · 五人 ごにん …

The first two are completely irregular and are among the first words anyone learns. 四人 is よにん, not よんにん.

**～本(ほん) — long thin things.** Pens, bottles, trees, umbrellas, bananas, roads, and telephone calls.

一本 **いっぽん** · 二本 にほん · 三本 **さんぼん** · 四本 よんほん · 六本 **ろっぽん** · 八本 **はっぽん** · 十本 **じゅっぽん**

**～枚(まい) — flat thin things.** Paper, shirts, plates, tickets, stamps, CDs. Beautifully regular: 一枚、二枚、三枚…

**～匹(ひき) — small animals.** Cats, dogs, fish, insects.

一匹 **いっぴき** · 三匹 **さんびき** · 六匹 **ろっぴき** · 八匹 **はっぴき** · 十匹 **じゅっぴき**

**The pattern across all of them.** A counter starting with は行 (本, 匹, 杯) changes to ぱ行 after 1, 6, 8, 10 and to ば行 after 3. Learn that shape once and three counters come with it; learning thirty separate irregularities is the alternative.

**Big animals take ～頭(とう)** and birds take ～羽(わ). You will need them rarely.

**Practice.** Say: three people · two bottles of beer (ビール) · five sheets of paper (紙, かみ) · one cat (猫, ねこ). Answers: 三人 · ビールを二本 · 紙を五枚 · 猫が一匹。
Telling the time:
Hours take 時(じ) and minutes take 分(ふん/ぷん). Both have irregular readings, and they are in the common numbers rather than the rare ones.

**Hours — ～時**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1時 いちじ | 2時 にじ | 3時 さんじ | **4時 よじ** |
| 5時 ごじ | 6時 ろくじ | **7時 しちじ** | 8時 はちじ |
| **9時 くじ** | 10時 じゅうじ | 11時 じゅういちじ | 12時 じゅうにじ |

4, 7 and 9 use the older readings — よじ, しちじ, くじ — and never よんじ, ななじ or きゅうじ.

**Minutes — ～分**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 1分 **いっぷん** | 2分 にふん |
| 3分 **さんぷん** | 4分 **よんぷん** |
| 5分 ごふん | 6分 **ろっぷん** |
| 7分 ななふん | 8分 **はっぷん** |
| 9分 きゅうふん | 10分 **じゅっぷん** |

The same は→ぱ pattern after 1, 6, 8, 10, plus 3 and 4 here.

**Half past is 半(はん):** 三時半 — half past three.

**Morning and afternoon go in front:** 午前(ごぜん) and 午後(ごご). 午後三時 — 3pm. The 24-hour clock is used for timetables.

**Asking:** 今(いま)何時ですか。 — What time is it now?

**から and まで** give a span: 九時から五時まで — from nine to five.

**Practice.** Say the current time. Then: 4:00, 7:30, 9:15, 10:45, from 2 to 6. Answers: よじ · しちじはん · くじじゅうごふん · じゅうじよんじゅうごふん · にじからろくじまで。
Days, months and dates:
Dates are where Japanese keeps most of its irregular readings, and there is no way round learning them.

**Months are regular.** 月(がつ) after the number: 一月 いちがつ, 二月 にがつ … 十二月 じゅうにがつ. The only traps are **四月 しがつ**, **七月 しちがつ** and **九月 くがつ** — the older readings again.

**Days of the month are not regular.** The first ten, plus a few later ones, use native readings:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1日 **ついたち** | 2日 ふつか | 3日 みっか | 4日 よっか |
| 5日 いつか | 6日 むいか | 7日 なのか | 8日 ようか |
| 9日 ここのか | 10日 **とおか** | 14日 じゅうよっか | 20日 **はつか** |
| 24日 にじゅうよっか | | | |

Everything else is the number plus にち: 11日 じゅういちにち, 15日 じゅうごにち.

**ついたち and はつか are the two to drill.** They look nothing like their numbers and they come up constantly.

**Days of the week** all end in 曜日(ようび):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 月曜日 げつようび | Monday |
| 火曜日 かようび | Tuesday |
| 水曜日 すいようび | Wednesday |
| 木曜日 もくようび | Thursday |
| 金曜日 きんようび | Friday |
| 土曜日 どようび | Saturday |
| 日曜日 にちようび | Sunday |

The kanji are moon, fire, water, wood, metal, earth, sun — the same scheme as the planets behind the English names.

**Order is big to small:** 2026年10月13日 — year, month, day. The opposite of British order and the same as ISO.

**Practice.** Say today's date in full. Then your birthday. Then: the 1st, the 8th, the 14th, the 20th.
Verbs: the three groups, and how to tell:
Every Japanese verb belongs to one of three groups, and the group decides how it conjugates. Telling them apart is the whole of this lesson, because everything about verbs from here depends on it.

**Group 2 — る-verbs** (also called *ichidan*). The dictionary form ends in **る**, and the vowel before it is **い** or **え**:

食べる (taberu, to eat) · 見る (miru, to see) · 寝る (neru, to sleep) · 起きる (okiru, to get up)

These are the easy ones: drop る and add the ending.

**Group 1 — う-verbs** (*godan*). Everything else — any verb ending in う く ぐ す つ ぬ ぶ む, and any る-verb whose preceding vowel is あ, う or お:

飲む (nomu, to drink) · 行く (iku, to go) · 話す (hanasu, to speak) · 作る (tsukuru, to make) · 分かる (wakaru, to understand)

These change the final vowel before adding the ending.

**Group 3 — the two irregulars.** する (to do) and 来る (くる, to come). That is the entire group. する also attaches to nouns to make verbs — 勉強する, 電話する — so it appears constantly.

**The trap.** Some verbs end in る with い or え before it and are still group 1:

| Verb | Looks like | Actually |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 帰る (かえる, to return) | group 2 | **group 1** |
| 入る (はいる, to enter) | group 2 | **group 1** |
| 走る (はしる, to run) | group 2 | **group 1** |
| 知る (しる, to know) | group 2 | **group 1** |
| 切る (きる, to cut) | group 2 | **group 1** |

There are perhaps a dozen of these in common use and they are learned individually. A dictionary marks the group; so does the card for each verb in the deck.

**Practice.** Sort these: 書く(かく), 食べる, 見る, 読む(よむ), する, 帰る, 寝る, 来る, 泳ぐ(およぐ). Answers — group 1: 書く, 読む, 帰る, 泳ぐ. Group 2: 食べる, 見る, 寝る. Group 3: する, 来る.
ます — the polite form:
The polite present-and-future form of a verb, and the one you will use in almost every sentence for a long time.

**Group 2 (る-verbs): drop る, add ます.**

食べる → 食べ**ます** · 見る → 見**ます** · 寝る → 寝**ます**

**Group 1 (う-verbs): change the final う-sound to its い-sound, then add ます.**

| Dictionary | Change | ます form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 飲**む** | む → み | 飲**みます** |
| 行**く** | く → き | 行**きます** |
| 話**す** | す → し | 話**します** |
| 待**つ** | つ → ち | 待**ちます** |
| 作**る** | る → り | 作**ります** |
| 買**う** | う → **い** | 買**います** |

The last one is the only oddity: う becomes い, not わ. 買う → 買います.

**Group 3: learn them.** する → **します** · 来る → **来ます** (きます)

**ます covers present and future.** 食べます is "I eat", "I will eat" and "I am going to eat". Which one is decided by context or by a time word — 明日食べます is clearly future. Japanese has no separate future tense, and this is the first place that matters.

**ます is polite, not formal.** It is the normal register for talking to anyone who is not a close friend, and it is never wrong. The plain forms come later in this stage; they are for friends, for writing, and for building other grammar on top of.

**Practice.** Put these into ます form: 読む, 書く, 見る, 行く, 話す, する, 来る, 食べる, 買う, 待つ. Answers: 読みます, 書きます, 見ます, 行きます, 話します, します, 来ます, 食べます, 買います, 待ちます。
ません, ました, ませんでした:
All four polite forms of a verb, from the one ending you already know. The stem never changes — only what comes after ます.

| | Non-past | Past |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | 食べ**ます** | 食べ**ました** |
| Negative | 食べ**ません** | 食べ**ませんでした** |

- 毎日(まいにち)コーヒーを飲みます。 — I drink coffee every day.
- 今日は飲みません。 — I'm not drinking any today.
- 昨日飲みました。 — I drank some yesterday.
- 先週(せんしゅう)は飲みませんでした。 — I didn't drink any last week.

**This is the whole polite conjugation.** Once a verb is in ます form, these three are automatic — there is nothing further to learn per verb. That is why ます form is where the deck stores verbs alongside the dictionary form.

**ませんでした is long and it is correct.** There is no shorter polite past negative. In plain speech it becomes なかった, which is much shorter, and that is part of why plain forms are worth having later.

**Answering a negative question.** Japanese はい and いいえ agree with the *question*, not with the fact:

- 食べませんか。 — Aren't you eating?
- **はい**、食べません。 — That's right, I'm not.

English says "no, I'm not"; Japanese says "yes, that's correct". This reverses often enough to be worth noticing now.

**Practice.** Take 行きます, 見ます, します and 読みます through all four forms. Then answer in Japanese: 昨日、日本語を勉強しましたか。
を — the object particle:
を marks the direct object: the thing the verb acts on. It is written を and said ***o***, identically to お, and it is never used for anything else.

- パンを食べます。 — I eat bread.
- 日本語を勉強します。 — I study Japanese.
- 本を読みました。 — I read a book.

**It is only ever a particle.** You will never find を inside a word. Seeing it means the word before it is an object.

**Typing it** is `wo` on an IME, despite the pronunciation.

**Verbs of motion take を for the path travelled** — this is the one use that is not a direct object and it surprises people:

- 公園(こうえん)を散歩(さんぽ)します。 — I walk through the park.
- 橋(はし)を渡(わた)ります。 — I cross the bridge.

The park is not being acted on; it is the space passed through. 道を歩く, 空を飛ぶ — same pattern.

**Some verbs that take an object in English do not in Japanese.** 分かる (to understand) takes が, not を: 日本語**が**分かります. So does 好き, and 上手, and several others — they are grammatically descriptions rather than actions. That group gets its own lesson shortly.

**を is replaced by は or も**, never joined to them. "I eat bread too" is パン**も**食べます, not パンをも.

**Practice.** Build: I drink water (水, みず). · I watch television (テレビ). · I bought a car (車, くるま). · I cross the bridge. Answers: 水を飲みます。 · テレビを見ます。 · 車を買いました。 · 橋を渡ります。
に — the particle of destination, time an:
に has several jobs and they are related closely enough to learn together: it marks a **point** — in space, in time, or of arrival.

**1. Destination.** With 行く, 来る, 帰る:

東京**に**行きます。 — I'm going to Tokyo.

**2. A specific point in time.** With clock times, dates, days:

七時**に**起きます。 — I get up at seven.
月曜日**に**行きます。 — I'll go on Monday.

**に is not used with vague time words.** 今日、明日、毎日、来週 take no particle at all: 明日行きます, never 明日に. The rule is that に goes with times you could point at on a calendar or a clock, and not with relative ones.

**3. Existence.** With あります and います:

机の上**に**本があります。 — There is a book on the desk.

**4. The recipient.** Who something is given or said to:

田中さん**に**手紙(てがみ)を書きました。 — I wrote a letter to Tanaka.

**5. Purpose, with a motion verb.** Verb stem + に + 行く:

映画(えいが)を見**に**行きます。 — I'm going to see a film.

**The one to watch is に versus で**, which is the next lesson. Shorthand: に is where something *is* or *ends up*; で is where something *happens*.

**Practice.** Fill in に where it belongs: 明日__学校__行きます。 · 六時__起きます。 · 来週__東京__行きます。 Answers: 明日(no particle)学校に行きます。 · 六時に起きます。 · 来週(no particle)東京に行きます。
で — where something happens, and what wi:
で marks the **place an action happens** and the **means by which** it happens. It is the particle most often confused with に, and the distinction is sharp once stated.

**1. Where an action takes place.**

図書館**で**勉強します。 — I study at the library.
レストラン**で**食べました。 — I ate at a restaurant.

**2. By what means.**

電車(でんしゃ)**で**行きます。 — I go by train.
